chapter: Chicago, Ohio and Jelly Roll Morton
title: Freddy Jenkins, joining Local 802 and the Joe Steele job
summary: Friend Freddy Jenkins cannot lend the fifty-dollar union fee, so Thomas plays two weeks at pianist Joe Steele's Seventh Avenue club while the union man is away and then pays to join Local 802.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: See, that's when... I left my... I made the mistake of leaving my transfer in. It wasn't no mistake in the end...
Your transfer out where?

In New York. Because when I went out on the road with Jelly, I didn't take my transfer up. So I come in town, and the only musician I knew was Freddy Jenkins. I don't know how we got to be such friends, but anyway...
Freddy Jenkins was a trumpet player.
A trumpet player, yeah.
He was with Duke Ellington's band.
Right.
Was he with Duke then?
Yeah, he was with Duke then.
Thomas - 67
So how did you know him?
I don't know. I just got to meet...
He lives in Texas, doesn't he? [F. JENKINS WAS BORN IN NYC, 1906]
Yeah.
I (?) ran into him down in Texas...
A guy told me later on... I got a story to tell about him. A guy told me later that Freddy Jenkins wanted to be a big guy. He was little when I first met him.
He was a very tiny man, a small little man...

Yeah, but he got to be big. And he came to see me when I was playing with Cab. Because we got to be good friends. I needed fifty dollars to join the union, and the only one I had nerve enough to ask was Freddy -- and Freddy didn't have no money. And I got this job. When I came back to New York, I was surprised. The guy said, 'Man, where have you been? We've been looking for you.' I didn't know I'd made no impression in New York! So this guy named Joe Steele...
A drummer.
No, a pianist.
Piano player! Yeah, Joe Steele.
He was a genius. He played 'Rhapsody In Blue' better than (?). He played 'Rhapsody in Blue' better
Thomas - 68
than anybody. Couldn't nobody play "Rhapsody In Blue" no better than Joe Steele.
He was around for a long time.
Yeah. And he was a little off...
Yeah.

...but he could play the piano. And he could write. But he didn't know how to write for saxophone. Man, he'd write some parts up there where your fingers would be twisting. He could play that on piano, but some things you don't write for saxophone players to play way up high. But I scuffled and played them.

And he got this job at a little club up on Seventh Avenue... I found out that the union man, Minton, had gone on vacation, and he'd be gone for two weeks. So that meant there wasn't nobody who'd be checking the places up in Harlem. So I went down to the union to put in my transfer, and the man said, "You can't put in no transfer." He went out and checked my records (and I left my transfer), and he said, "You got to join!" I said, "Join? I ain't got a (?)quarter to one(?)." So as I said, I left and I went uptown and found out that Minton was out of town, so I played them two weeks and I saved me twenty-five dollars a week, and I come down there the next and put my fifty dollars down. That's how I joined the union. And once I
Thomas - 69
got in...
What year was that, Foots?
That was around '27. '27 or '28. So that job didn't last too long.
